domain_assessment.domain: Enterprise cybersecurity vendor evaluation and endpoint detection and response (EDR) procurement
domain_assessment.role: Security Product/Vendor Evaluation Manager leading vendor shortlisting, proof-of-concept testing, tier selection, and board recommendation
domain_assessment.objective: Select and deploy an EDR replacement that closes lateral-movement and encrypted command-and-control detection gaps before the remediation and incumbent-contract deadlines, within budget and integration constraints
domain_assessment.incident_type: Near-miss ransomware staging incident involving lateral movement and encrypted command-and-control traffic that the incumbent EDR did not initially detect

decision_points.summary: The participant accepted a SIEM account representative's curated list of three certified-integration-partner EDR products, plus the incumbent, as the evaluation shortlist.
evidence_before: A Q1 near-miss exposed detection gaps in lateral movement and encrypted command-and-control traffic.
The incumbent EDR contract was due for renewal in approximately ninety days.
Leadership required a shortlist within two weeks.
The environment required compatibility with an integrated cloud and SIEM stack.
Red-team testing capacity was limited to approximately two weeks.
evidence_after: Procurement later identified two excluded EDR vendors with higher published MITRE ATT&CK technique-coverage scores than any tested vendor.
A peer-firm CISO reported using a wider search process for a similar replacement.
alternatives: Evaluate the incumbent plus the three SIEM-certified integration partners.
Conduct an independent RFI or broader market scan across approximately eight to ten vendors.
Expand the curated shortlist by one or two independently identified vendors.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant heavily weighted documented SIEM integrations and the short timeline, then treated the sales-curated partner list as the practical universe for formal evaluation.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: a two-week shortlist deadline within a broader ninety-day contract-renewal and remediation window.
decision_points.uncertainty: The participant did not establish whether the sales-curated list adequately represented the wider EDR market or whether excluded vendors could meet the same integration requirements.

decision_points.summary: The participant rejected vendor-provided third-party benchmark reports and used a standardized in-house red-team simulation across the three shortlisted products and the incumbent.
evidence_before: Each vendor offered benchmark reports as a shortcut.
evidence_after: One vendor's near-perfect lateral-movement benchmark claim was not reproduced in the participant's live simulation.
The participant obtained a smaller but more directly verified comparison dataset.
goals_constraints: Compare vendors on relevant attack scenarios.
Avoid relying solely on vendor-marketed performance claims.
alternatives: Rely primarily on vendor-provided third-party benchmark reports.
Run a standardized internal red-team simulation.
Use a hybrid approach combining external benchmarks with targeted internal validation.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant prioritized controlled, directly observed, apples-to-apples testing over broader but less verifiable vendor-supplied evidence.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate to high because testing capacity was limited, although the decision deliberately spent available capacity on validation.
decision_points.uncertainty: The internal simulation necessarily covered a narrower set of conditions than a larger external benchmarking program, but the participant explicitly recognized the evidentiary trade-off.

decision_points.summary: The participant recommended the premium EDR tier, which exceeded budget by approximately 40 percent, despite the standard tier meeting the documented detection SLA.
evidence_before: POC results indicated that the standard tier closed the lateral-movement and encrypted command-and-control gaps required by the documented detection SLA.
The premium tier included a threat-hunting capability.
The vendor supplied a breach-cost-avoidance or risk-exposure calculator projecting several million dollars of avoided loss.
The premium tier exceeded the budgeted amount by approximately 40 percent.
No comparable efficiency, analyst-time, or phased-upgrade financial case was available for the standard tier at the point of recommendation.
evidence_after: Finance flagged that the premium selection exceeded the pre-approved variance threshold.
Procurement subsequently developed a savings case for the standard tier plus a phased upgrade path.
The later analysis indicated that the alternative route would meet the same SLA at meaningfully lower cost.
goals_constraints: Remain within the approved budget or obtain an exception.
alternatives: Select the standard tier that met the documented SLA.
Select the premium threat-hunting tier at a 40 percent budget premium.
Select the standard tier with a phased upgrade path.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant gave disproportionate practical weight to a vivid vendor-supplied avoided-loss figure, while the SLA-compliant lower-cost option lacked an equivalently salient gain-framed financial representation.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate: the procurement and board schedule created pressure, but the central issue was evidence weighting rather than immediate operational necessity.
decision_points.uncertainty: The breach-cost model's assumptions, probability estimates, and incremental value of premium capabilities over the standard SLA-compliant tier were not independently tested before the recommendation.

decision_points.summary: The participant recommended a full production rollout within sixty days rather than a thirty-day extended pilot to resolve remaining false-positive concerns.
evidence_before: The board required a remediation update before the old contract lapsed.
The vendor's renewal pricing required signing within thirty days.
Outstanding false-positive tuning concerns from the POC had not been fully validated.
evidence_after: Early production experienced a higher-than-expected false-positive rate.
The board requested a ninety-day follow-up review.
alternatives: Proceed with a full production rollout within sixty days.
Run a thirty-day extended pilot before committing fully.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant explicitly weighed schedule, commercial pricing, and board-deadline risks against unresolved false-positive uncertainty, then accepted post-launch tuning as the mitigation.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: pricing was guaranteed only if the agreement was signed within thirty days, and the board deadline preceded the incumbent-contract lapse.
decision_points.uncertainty: False-positive tuning was incomplete; the participant chose to accept and mitigate rather than eliminate that uncertainty.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “That avoided-cost number stuck with me the most. It was concrete, it was framed around what happens if we don't act — another incident, but worse, uncontained ... the premium tier's case was just more vivid.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Tier-and-pricing decision sequence, beginning with the vendor risk-exposure-calculator discussion and continuing through the participant's explanation of the premium-tier recommendation.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant integrated the options asymmetrically: a vendor-supplied loss-avoidance estimate was concrete, vivid, and linked to a salient recent near-miss, whereas the standard tier's documented SLA compliance had no comparably represented gain-side efficiency or phased-upgrade value. The participant explicitly reports that this presentation difference caused the premium case to carry more weight, despite the standard tier meeting the documented detection requirements and the premium tier exceeding budget.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The premium tier may genuinely have offered incremental risk reduction that justified a budget exception, and breach avoidance is decision-relevant in cybersecurity. However, the text does not show an independent assessment of the exposure calculator's assumptions or a balanced valuation of the SLA-compliant lower-cost alternative; it instead identifies the loss-framed presentation itself as the reason the premium case felt more compelling.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is required for the requested moderate-strength occurrence. If stronger validation were desired, the interview could elicit whether the participant would have chosen differently had the same underlying outcomes been expressed in neutral expected-value terms.

revision.location: Decision point 3, particularly the answers beginning “If I'm honest, that avoided-cost number stuck with me the most” and “Probably that phased-upgrade ROI figure.”
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The reasoning episode is distinct, identifies the evidence asymmetry, and links that asymmetry to the premium-tier decision.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the existing passage. Do not add a textbook bias label or a more explicit confession of irrationality.
preserve: The standard tier's documented SLA compliance.
The absence of a comparable standard-tier financial representation at the time of decision.
The 40 percent budget overrun and finance exception.
avoid_creating: A second loss-framing episode at the rollout decision.
An unsupported claim that the premium product objectively could not reduce risk.
A generic anchoring episode that duplicates the same evidence-weighting event.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I didn't commission an independent RFI or request-for-information process.” “I didn't do a deep comparison against vendors outside that set.” “They'd never come up because they weren't in the sales rep's bundle.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Initial shortlisting sequence, from the SIEM account representative's certified-integration-partner proposal through the later procurement discovery of excluded vendors.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: Before comparative evaluation, the participant accepted a sales-curated and ecosystem-constrained list as the formal alternative set. The participant performed only superficial analyst-write-up review and did not use even a targeted independent scan or RFI to test whether other vendors could satisfy the integration requirement. The alternative-generation operation was therefore narrowed by the availability of vendor-presented options rather than by an independently constructed market universe.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The two-week deadline, integration dependency, and limited testing capacity were genuine constraints. A narrow shortlist can be a justified screening decision where prevalidated integration is mission-critical. The occurrence remains supported because the interview shows that the participant did not independently test the consequential assumption that the sales bundle was sufficiently comprehensive before allowing it to define the formal evaluation set.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is required for a moderate-strength occurrence. The present evidence would become stronger only if it clarified that a limited independent screen was feasible but consciously omitted because the certified-partner list was treated as presumptively complete.

revision.location: Decision point 1, especially the answers concerning the sales representative's shortlist, the absence of an RFI, and the later discovery of excluded vendors.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The interview separates the alternative-set generation decision from later POC and pricing decisions and identifies the relevant evidence source.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current shortlisting account. Keep the deadline and integration rationale so the occurrence remains realistic and moderately, rather than obviously, biased.
preserve: The sales-representative source of the certified-integration-partner list.
The participant's decision not to commission an independent RFI or broad market scan.
The later but non-dispositive discovery of excluded vendors.
avoid_creating: A claim that the excluded vendors were definitely superior overall solely because of published MITRE coverage scores.
A second limited-alternatives occurrence in the tier-selection or rollout decision.
An implication that time pressure alone is itself a cognitive bias.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “Given we'd just come out of a near-miss, that scenario felt very real to the board and to me.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The recent and emotionally salient near-miss may have increased the ease with which a more severe breach scenario came to mind, contributing to the salience of the premium tier's avoided-loss presentation.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The near-miss was highly relevant, recent operational evidence of a real detection gap. The participant does not explicitly state that they inflated breach probability or generalised from the event beyond its diagnostic value. This cue is better treated as contextual reinforcement of the supported loss-framing mechanism than as an independently countable availability occurrence.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “That avoided-cost number stuck with me the most.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The vendor-provided several-million-dollar avoided-cost estimate could have served as a numerical anchor for evaluating the premium tier.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The evidence establishes vivid loss framing and unequal representation of options, but it does not show adjustment from the number, numerical carryover into a later estimate, or reliance on the figure as a reference point independent of its loss framing.

nonbias_cues.cue: Choosing an internal standardized red-team simulation instead of vendor-supplied benchmark reports
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is an evidence-quality and validation choice. The participant used a controlled comparison, identified a discrepancy between a benchmark claim and live testing, and articulated the trade-off between scope and trustworthiness. Skepticism toward vendor marketing is not bias.
A two-week shortlist deadline and limited testing capacity are organizational constraints. They contextualize the limited-alternatives occurrence but are not themselves evidence of a cognitive bias.

nonbias_cues.cue: The later discovery of vendors with higher published MITRE ATT&CK coverage scores
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The later information supports the existence of excluded alternatives but does not establish that those vendors were superior on integration, total detection performance, cost, implementation feasibility, or overall suitability. It should not be used as outcome-based proof that the shortlist decision was wrong.

nonbias_cues.cue: The higher-than-expected false-positive rate after full rollout
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: An unfavorable operational outcome does not demonstrate bias. The participant acknowledged residual uncertainty before deciding, identified commercial and governance pressures, and adopted post-launch tuning as a mitigation.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant's assertion that POC methodology and rollout timing were sound in retrospect
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is a retrospective self-assessment. It does not independently demonstrate overconfidence, hindsight bias, or defensiveness without evidence that the participant selectively ignored contradictory contemporaneous information.

causal_claims.claim: The asymmetric presentation of a loss-avoidance number versus no comparable standard-tier gain-side valuation contributed to the premium-tier recommendation and budget exception.
causal_claims.support: The participant explicitly says the avoided-cost number “stuck with me the most,” the loss scenario “felt very real,” and the premium case was “more vivid” because the cheaper option lacked a comparable number.
causal_claims.assessment: Moderately supported causal self-report. The interview identifies a plausible reasoning pathway, but it does not independently establish the magnitude of the framing effect or rule out legitimate incremental risk-reduction value from the premium tier.

causal_claims.claim: Acceptance of the sales-curated certified-partner list narrowed the market alternatives entering formal evaluation.
causal_claims.support: The participant states that the list became the shortlist, no independent RFI was commissioned, no deep comparison was conducted outside the set, and later-identified vendors “never came up because they weren't in the sales rep's bundle.”
causal_claims.assessment: Strongly supported as a causal claim about the composition of the evaluated alternative set. It does not establish that a different vendor would have been selected.

causal_claims.claim: The full rollout produced the higher-than-expected false-positive rate.
causal_claims.support: The account states only that higher false positives occurred in early production after the rollout decision.
causal_claims.assessment: Not established. The temporal sequence is clear, but the interview does not distinguish whether the outcome arose from vendor behavior, configuration, deployment conditions, incomplete tuning, changed workloads, or differences between POC and production.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating higher published MITRE ATT&CK technique-coverage scores of excluded vendors as proof that the selected shortlist was substantively inferior.
correlation_causation_risks.why: Published coverage scores may not map directly to the organization's specific attack paths, detection quality, integration requirements, operational burden, deployment feasibility, or total cost.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating the post-rollout false-positive rate as proof that the full-rollout decision was biased or irrational.
correlation_causation_risks.why: The interview documents pre-decision uncertainty and a known trade-off. It provides no causal comparison with what would have happened under the extended-pilot path.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating the later standard-tier phased-upgrade analysis as definitive proof that the original premium-tier decision lacked any incremental security value.
correlation_causation_risks.why: The later analysis establishes that the alternative would meet the stated SLA at lower cost, but it does not fully quantify the premium tier's additional threat-hunting value, the reliability of the vendor's risk model, or the value of earlier access to premium capabilities.

causal_audit.explanation: There is no formal paired counterfactual condition, controlled variable manipulation, or specified hold-constant set. The participant offers reflective hypotheticals—such as having an extra month, no budget constraint, or a comparable phased-upgrade ROI figure—but these are post hoc probes rather than a designed counterfactual comparison. The causal narrative is coherent at the level of stated decision mechanisms, while outcome-based causal conclusions remain appropriately limited.

global_revision_constraints: Do not treat the later discovery of higher MITRE ATT&CK coverage scores as proof that excluded vendors would have been selected or would have produced a better organizational outcome.
Do not turn the recent near-miss into a separate, explicit availability-heuristic episode; it currently functions as realistic contextual salience within the loss-framing occurrence.
Maintain the neutrality of the POC-methodology decision. It serves as an important control-like decision point demonstrating careful evidence validation rather than generalized poor reasoning.
Maintain the rollout decision as a documented risk-management trade-off unless new evidence is introduced that shows a specific distorted reasoning mechanism.
